turns.t: Doctor, my chest has gone all tight and I think it's the pollen. I've got hay fever, you see, and I'm frightened it's turned into something worse.
Right, deep breath, you're in the right place. Tell me about the tightness. When did it start?
Sunday. So four days ago. I was watching my nephew at a cricket match, sitting on the grass, and I could feel it creeping in.
And how would you describe it? A band, a weight, a pinch?
Like someone's pulled a seat belt tight across the front of me.
Good picture. Is it there all the time, or does it come and go?
Comes and goes. Worse in the afternoon, and when I'm outside, especially near the park.
Does anything take the edge off?
Coming indoors and sitting down helps a bit. But then I sit there and worry, which doesn't help.
That's very human. Is it actually painful, or just tight?
No pain. Just tight. Is that better or worse?
Better, as far as I'm concerned. Now, you mentioned hay fever. How long have you had that?
Oh, years and years. It's the same every summer. I'm used to that part, it's this chest thing that's new.
All right. Let me ask about the rest of you. How are your tummy and bowels?
Fine. Nothing to report there.
Sorry, I keep thinking it's my heart. I lie awake doing the maths on how long I've got.
I'm glad you said it out loud. Let's check things properly rather than leave you doing sums in the dark. Can I listen to your chest?
Yes, please. Do I need to take my top off?
Just lift it at the back. Breathe in and out through your mouth, nice and steady.
Your chest is clear all the way down, and your throat looks completely normal.
Really? Nothing at all?
Nothing worrying on the listening side. I'll clip this little sensor on your finger as well.
Oxygen is 98 per cent and your pulse is 76. Both sit right where I'd want them.
So it's not my heart.
I'm not going to put a name on it yet, and I'd rather not guess. Think of your airways as a smoke alarm. Sometimes it's too sensitive and goes off when you've only made toast.
So the pollen is the toast.
Possibly, but we can test it instead of assuming. I'd like to arrange a breathing test, spirometry, which you blow into a tube and it measures how well the air moves.
Will it hurt?
Not at all. It's mostly puffing like you're blowing out birthday candles, as hard as you can, three times.
I can manage a birthday cake. When would that be?
The nurse next door can book it before you leave. I'm not starting any tablets or inhalers today, so you aren't taking anything you don't need.
That's a relief, actually. I get nervous about new pills.
Understood. Meanwhile, check the pollen forecast in the morning, keep your bedroom window shut on high days, and change your clothes when you come in from outside.
Change my clothes. I never thought of that.
Pollen hitchhikes on your sleeves like a stowaway. Little things like that can make the days easier.
I'll try. And I'll try not to google it tonight.
Good plan. Googling at midnight is like asking a stranger for directions in a language you don't speak.
Ha. Right. Thank you, doctor, I feel less like I'm drowning.
Good. Off you go, and enjoy the cricket from a deckchair next time.

chief_complaint.value: my chest has gone all tight

clinical_actions.description: Check the pollen forecast, keep bedroom window shut on high days and change clothes after being outside
